titolo: What Did Ordinary Families Actually Eat During the Great Depression?
descrizione: What did ordinary American families really eat during the Great Depression? This documentary follows one day at the table, from breakfast to supper, through real photographs, soup kitchens, pellagra, the 1933 pig slaughter, boxed macaroni, Depression cake and the first food stamps of 1939. Sources are listed below.

scene.testo: If your mother ever sent you for bread,
you knew the change was never yours.
In the 1930s, millions of children knew that rule.
Every penny at the table had a job.
This is one day of eating, breakfast to supper.
We'll sit at real tables, in real places.
One was run by a famous gangster.
One meal came in a cardboard box for nineteen cents.
And one table was paid for with blue stamps.
But that's not the strangest part of the story.
In 1933, America destroyed millions of baby pigs,
while people went hungry. The reason will surprise you.
Let's begin where every day began: early, and hungry.
March, 1936. Nipomo, California.
A photographer named Dorothea Lange was driving home.
She had spent a month photographing farm workers.
She was tired, and the road home was long.
She drove right past a sign for a pea pickers' camp.
Then, about twenty miles later, she turned the car around.
In the camp she found a mother and her children.
Lange took only six photographs.
She worked fast, and she did not ask the woman's name.
Lange wrote down what the family was eating.
Frozen vegetables from the surrounding fields,
and birds the children had killed.
The pea crop had frozen, so there was no work.
No work meant no wages. No wages meant no groceries.
Her photograph ran in a San Francisco newspaper.
Soon afterward, the government sent food to the camp.
By then, the family had already moved on.
The picture became known as Migrant Mother.
Decades later, the woman was identified: Florence Owens Thompson.
If your grandmother never wasted a crust of bread,
she probably learned that in those years.
Noon. Chicago. Thanksgiving Day, 1930.
A line of men stretched down South State Street.
They were waiting for a free hot meal.
The kitchen belonged to Al Capone.
Newspapers said it fed thousands of people that day.
Soup, bread, and coffee.
Critics called it public relations for a gangster.
Whatever his motives, the hunger was real.
Across the country, cities opened bread lines.
Churches and charities ran most of them.
A bowl of soup could be a man's only meal.
By 1933, about one worker in four had no job.
Many had worked all their lives, and felt ashamed.
Men held their hats and waited quietly.
Few spoke much while they stood in the line.
Behind every man in line stood a family at home.
Some men carried bread home to their children.
If your grandfather never complained about plain food,
he probably learned that in those years.
Midday. Pie Town, New Mexico, 1940.
A man named Clyde Norman sold pies here.
The town took its name from the pies.
It sits along U.S. Highway 60, far from any city.
Homesteaders arrived from the dry southern plains.
Many were running from drought and dust.
On Black Sunday, April 1935, a dust cloud swallowed towns.
In Pie Town, they tried to start over.
They built their own cabins, and dug their own wells.
Pinto beans were the crop that held it together.
Photographer Russell Lee came to document them.
He worked for the Farm Security Administration.
His pictures show families at dinner and at work.
One family, the Caudills, grew beans and ate them too.
Neighbors gathered for dances, and for church.
Those photographs sit today in the Library of Congress.
Cooks sewed dresses from printed flour sacks.
Nothing came into the house without a second use.
If your grandmother saved every flour sack,
she probably learned it in those years.
Late afternoon, in the South, a quieter hunger.
Many poor families lived on cornmeal, molasses, and fatback.
Doctors called it the three M's: meat, meal, molasses.
That diet caused a disease called pellagra.
It brought rashes, weakness, confusion, and sometimes death.
In the South, it killed thousands of people every year.
It often flared up in spring and summer.
Many people believed it was a germ.
Dr. Joseph Goldberger said it was the diet.
In 1915, he tested it on Mississippi prisoners.
They volunteered in exchange for a promised pardon.
Volunteers eating the poor diet fell ill.
In 1937, scientists found that niacin cured it.
Soon after, flour and bread were enriched with it.
In early spring, wild greens filled the gaps.
Dandelion leaves and poke salad cost nothing to gather.
Some families hunted rabbits, squirrels, and possum.
In Texas, some called armadillos Hoover hogs.
It was a bitter joke aimed at the president.
Empty pockets turned inside out were Hoover flags.
If your grandmother cooked weeds with a bit of bacon,
she probably learned it in those years.
Now the strange problem: too much food.
Prices were so low that crops barely paid.
In some places, farmers burned corn for fuel.
It was cheaper to burn than to haul to market.
In 1933, angry Iowa farmers dumped milk on roads.
That summer, the government launched a drastic plan.
The Department of Agriculture was led by Henry Wallace.
About six million young pigs were bought and killed.
The goal was to lift the price of pork.
The public was outraged while people went hungry.
So part of the pork went to relief families.
That fall, the government created a surplus relief agency.
Its job was to move farm surplus to the hungry.
Families lined up with sacks and baskets.
Abundance in the fields, scarcity in the kitchen.
Economists argued about it for years afterward.
Late afternoon. A mother needs something cheap and filling.
In 1937, a new box appeared on grocery shelves.
Kraft sold macaroni with a packet of cheese.
One box served four people.
The price was nineteen cents.
Ads promised a meal for four in minutes.
No refrigerator needed, and hardly any cooking skill.
The same year, Hormel launched a canned meat: Spam.
It could sit on a shelf for years.
Sliced bread had reached stores nationwide by 1930.
The Hershey bar stayed at five cents.
A nickel was a small luxury a child could afford.
Even the White House kept its meals plain.
Eleanor Roosevelt's housekeeper, Henrietta Nesbitt, ran the kitchen.
Her menus were so plain that guests joked about them.
In 1939, they served hot dogs to King George.
Boxed and canned foods made meals predictable.
And predictability was worth a lot to a worried mother.
If your family still loves boxed mac and cheese,
you are tasting a Depression-era habit.
Evening. Dessert, if there was any.
Eggs, milk, and butter were expensive.
So cooks invented a cake without any of them.
People called it wacky cake, or Depression cake.
Flour, sugar, cocoa, baking soda, oil, vinegar, water.
The vinegar reacted with the soda and made it rise.
No eggs required, and it still tasted like chocolate.
Recipes passed hand to hand, kitchen to kitchen.
Neighbors copied them onto cards and scraps of paper.
Newspapers and radio shows offered cheap menus.
Cooks stretched meat with bread, rice, and oatmeal.
Stale bread became pudding, or breadcrumbs.
Cooking grease was saved and used again.
Gardens turned lawns into rows of vegetables.
Women canned tomatoes, beans, and peaches by the dozen.
Nothing was thrown out while it could be eaten.
If your grandmother kept a jar of bacon grease,
she probably learned it in those years.
Now the strangest table, promised at the start.
May, 1939. Rochester, New York.
The first food stamp program began there.
A family on relief bought orange stamps.
Those could be spent on almost any food.
For every dollar of orange stamps,
they received fifty cents of blue stamps free.
Blue stamps only bought foods listed as surplus.
Eggs, butter, flour, fruit, vegetables, and more.
The idea solved two problems at once.
Hungry families ate, and farmers sold their extra food.
Grocers in the program took the stamps like cash.
Milo Perkins led the agency that ran the program.
It spread to more than a thousand counties.
Over its life, about twenty million people used it.
The program ended in 1943, when jobs returned.
But the idea would come back, decades later.
Night. The dishes are washed, and the lamp is low.
So what did ordinary families actually eat?
Beans, bread, potatoes, cornmeal, and whatever the garden gave.
Some ate wild greens, some ate at soup kitchens,
and some ate a boxed dinner for nineteen cents.
No two tables looked the same.
But almost all of them shared one thing.
They shared what little they had.
A neighbor's pot of beans could feed two houses.
Children learned to clean their plates without being told.
Many carried those habits for the rest of their lives.
They saved string, foil, jars, and leftovers.
If you ever wondered why grandparents never waste food,
now you know where that habit came from.
